one_liner: Lock-free, thread-cached proxy allocator for small (16-992B) game allocations; passes everything else through to CRT malloc.
what_it_does: smmalloc speeds up the multithreaded many-small-allocations/frees pattern common in game engines by handling only a configured set of small size buckets and routing everything else to a caller-supplied fallback allocator (CRT malloc in the reference sample). The API is C-style around an opaque sm_allocator handle: _sm_allocator_create/_destroy for the instance, per-thread _sm_allocator_thread_cache_create/_destroy, and _sm_malloc/_sm_free/_sm_realloc/_sm_msize for the operations. It is not a drop-in for operator new/malloc; you pick bucket count and pool size up front and wire it in as a proxy in front of your existing allocator.
how_it_is_fast: Each thread keeps a small local cache (stack of up to SMM_MAX_CACHE_ITEMS_COUNT items per bucket) so most alloc/free calls touch no shared state. When a thread cache misses, each size-class bucket is backed by a lock-free singly-linked freelist using an atomic tagged-index (tag+offset packed into a 64-bit head) compare-and-swap to avoid ABA races without a lock. No per-allocation header/metadata is stored, so overhead is near zero, matching the README's own ~40-cycles-per-op figure for cache hits. Bucket sizes are computed algorithmically (default piecewise-linear partitioning) instead of via a lookup table.
when_to_use: Multithreaded C++ game/engine code with many repeated small (roughly 16-992B under the default partitioning) allocations and frees, e.g. per-frame temporaries
You already have a general-purpose fallback allocator and just want a fast path for a handful of known hot small sizes
Console targets where the platform default heap is a bottleneck (shipped in Warface on PS4, Xbox One, Switch)
You can manage explicit thread-cache create/destroy calls as part of each worker thread's lifecycle
You're fine choosing bucket counts/size classes up front rather than using a fully general allocator
when_not_to_use: You need a true process-wide drop-in replacement for operator new/malloc (no LD_PRELOAD/global-override support; issue #5 requesting this is open, unresolved since 2022)
Your allocation sizes fall mostly outside the configured buckets — those pass straight through to the fallback allocator with no benefit
You need active upstream maintenance: no commits since 2023-10-13, and several issues (plain-C usage, LD_PRELOAD, Conan packaging) are open and unanswered
You need a pure C API/codebase — this is C++11 (templates, namespaces, std::atomic); issue #7 asking about plain-C use has no reply
You need independently reproduced numbers or a stated compiler/optimization-flag methodology — the README benchmark names hardware but not compiler or flags

integration.platforms: x86/x64; CI (GitHub Actions) builds and runs tests on Ubuntu and macOS with g++/clang++ and on Windows (Win32 and x64) with MSVC; also shipped on PS4 per README, though PS4 isn't in public CI
integration.thread_safety: Allocator instance and buckets are thread-safe via lock-free freelists with atomic tagged-index CAS; each thread must explicitly create and destroy its own thread-local cache (_sm_allocator_thread_cache_create/_destroy) around its use of the allocator
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same malloc/free/realloc-shaped verbs but proxy-only: only configured bucket sizes get the fast path, everything else is forwarded to a separate fallback allocator (CRT malloc in the sample)

gotchas: Must call _sm_allocator_thread_cache_create for every thread that allocates/frees through smmalloc and destroy it before the thread exits, or you lose the fast path or leak the cache
Bucket count and total pool size are fixed at _sm_allocator_create time; undersizing them silently routes more traffic to the fallback allocator with no error
The three bucket-size partitioning schemes (linear/piecewise-linear/float) are compile-time #defines, not runtime options — switching requires recompiling smmalloc
No per-allocation size/metadata is stored, so _sm_free/_sm_msize must be called against the same allocator instance that produced the pointer; mixing instances is undefined behavior
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick smmalloc over ltalloc or rpmalloc when you want a thin proxy layer restricted to a few known small size classes (e.g. per-frame game allocations) rather than a full malloc replacement; on the same i7-2600/CRT benchmark smmalloc's own reported numbers beat ltalloc (~3.9x vs ~2.6x CRT at 1 thread) and it has real console shipping history (Warface on PS4/X1/Switch) that the smaller general-purpose siblings don't claim.
verified_claims_summary: README's own (unreproduced, Tier C) tables show smmalloc's ops/sec beating CRT malloc/free on a multithreaded random 16-80B alloc/free stress test: ~3.9x at 1 thread and ~2.6x at 5 threads on Windows 10/i7-2600, and ~8.1x at 1 thread on PS4; neither table states the compiler or optimization flags used.
status_note: Maintenance is stale (no commits since 2023-10-13, and issues on LD_PRELOAD support and plain-C usage remain open and unanswered), but it's MIT-licensed, dependency-free, and small enough (4 source files) to vendor as-is.
